doc.title: Glenn Zottola interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, December 7, 2020

title: Atlantic City Jazz Festival at thirteen and playing without ambition
summary: At thirteen he played the Atlantic City festival; he describes jamming weekly with older Black musicians with no thought of making it.

story.theme_name: First paying gigs: getting started as a young professional
story.community_name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings

blocks.x: Before that, let me tell you, the next step after the Jack Teagarden/Bobby Hackett gig, my next big gig was when I was 13, the Atlantic City Jazz Festival. I was in a high school jazz band. I was only in grammar school or junior high and I was a lead trumpet and a jazz trumpet, and I went to this jazz band. Anyway I did the Atlantic City Jazz Festival on the bill with Dinah Washington, Gerry Mulligan, Oscar Peterson Trio, and Art Blakey. And I was 13. Yeah.

Well it sort of impacts my question here, because I remember when I was in high school and then music school, the circle of musician friends, we wanted to make it in the music business. And I can remember using that term. Oh we want to make it.
That’s a term that all the guys, young guys today, especially in the pop world, they haven’t even had a gig and they want to make it.
Yeah. So I wonder if you had that feeling. You might not have used that term.

I would get together every week jamming, guys a lot older than me, all the black cats in my neighborhood. And we’d get together and we’d jam with no thought of a gig, just to get together and play. Have a good time. There was never any thought of being famous or get a gig or whatever you know.
